masthead_title: The whole Treasury curve stays flagged for a fifth straight session as the front end eases only slightly off Monday's all-time record on the morning of the Fed's decision itself, oil pushes to a four-month high on a newly offline Saudi pipeline, and a scattered pre-vote tape sends Skyworks up 13.5% on an Apple read-through against a 10% Coinbase slide
provenance_note: Stated reasons and press framing via web search with named-source attribution (the standing source): Yahoo Finance, Investing.com, 24/7 Wall St., GuruFocus, TradingKey, Tradingpedia, StocksToTrade/Timothy Sykes, AAII, Al Jazeera, OilPrice.com, TradingEconomics, Kiplinger. No paid services used (Bigdata.com removed 2026-08-21).
regime_line: Every Treasury tenor this system tracks stays flagged for a fifth straight session — the 3-month bill, the maturity tied most directly to Fed policy, eased only slightly off Monday's all-time record to z +3.19 — hours before today's 2:00pm ET rate decision that markets price at roughly a 93% chance of a quarter-point hike to 3.75–4.00%.
claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — today's own decision is the live test, the AI-hardware claim keeps running hot, and a new claim opens on oil's supply story

Every open claim is checked against today's data before anything new is written (§4B). Yesterday is answered before today is asserted.

  • CL-0016 — cannot be reconciled this morning; today's 2:00pm ET decision is the test itself. This claim, opened yesterday, tests whether the 2-year Treasury yield (Monday 09-14's pre-decision close, 4.65%) moves 8bp or more in either direction by today's close. This system's pre-market pull only reaches Tuesday 09-15's close (2Y 4.67%, +2bp — inside the inconclusive band so far, unsurprising this many hours before the vote). Per §4E, this brief frames the decision rather than predicting it (see Today's calendar, below); reconciliation happens in tomorrow morning's run against today's actual close.
  • CL-0013 — stays open, no change. Fully reported already; remains open only because its own 2026-09-17 deadline hasn't passed.
  • CL-0015 — still open (due 2026-09-21), interim reading narrows slightly but stays past the confirm line. This claim tests whether the weekend AI-caution headlines mark a genuine AI-capex reassessment, using SMH's cumulative return against SPY from Friday 09-11's close (SMH 568.53, SPY 764.29) — a fall to -3 percentage points or worse over five trading days confirms. Two trading days in, the gap is -3.75pp (SMH -4.65%, SPY -0.90%) — slightly narrower than Monday's -4.31pp interim reading (SMH clawed back some ground Tuesday, +0.11%) but still past the confirm threshold, with three trading days left before the window closes. Interim, not a resolution.
  • CL-0017 opens this morning — on oil's fresh escalation (see Story and Tier 4, below): whether the newly reported Saudi pipeline outage marks a durable step-up in the supply-risk premium on top of the already-confirmed Iran/Strait-of-Hormuz story (CL-0007, confirmed 09-03), or a transient spike. Test: WTI (this system's series) closes at or above $100 through 2026-09-23 (confirms durable); a close back below $95 before then refutes it as transient.
story_html:
Reporting this morning centers on three threads. First, and dominant: today's Fed decision. Kiplinger and Yahoo Finance both report futures traders are pricing roughly a 93% probability of a 25-basis-point hike to a 3.75–4.00% target range at 2:00pm ET — the Fed's first hike since 2023 — with Chair Warsh's press conference and the updated dot plot (the Fed's own projections for where rates go next) following at 2:30pm. Second: Coinbase and other crypto-linked names sold off Tuesday — Investing.com and 24/7 Wall St. both report the trigger was a failed Senate cloture vote on the CLARITY Act (crypto market-structure legislation, stalling at 50-50, short of the 60 needed to proceed) compounded by Bitcoin and Ether declines and Fed-eve de-risking; Tradingpedia adds that some of Tuesday's move was pre-market and intensified through the session. Third: oil. Al Jazeera and OilPrice.com report Brent pushed to a four-month high as Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline — an alternative route around the Strait of Hormuz — remains offline after attacks last week, layering a fresh supply constraint on top of the Iran-linked disruption this system's claims ledger has tracked since late August (CL-0007). Underneath all three, a scattered stock-specific tape: Skyworks jumped 13.5% on Qorvo-merger progress and an Apple-foldable-iPhone supply read-through (Yahoo Finance, 24/7 Wall St., StocksToTrade), with Qualcomm (+4.2%) confirming the same chip-sector lift; Axon fell 9.8% on a $1 billion convertible-note offering (Tradingpedia) unrelated to any of the above.

Does the state file confirm the press's framing? On the Fed side, cleanly: every Treasury tenor stays flagged for a fifth straight session, and while the 3-month bill eased slightly off Monday's record (z +3.37 → +3.19), it remains this system's second-highest reading ever — entirely consistent with a hike priced as close to certain. On oil, also clean: WTI jumped 4.4% to $105.83, its own flag (z +1.59) confirming the reported supply story rather than a one-day headline spike (hence today's new CL-0017). Where the data complicates the tone of the morning's press coverage is breadth: Tuesday's equity weakness was broad rather than concentrated — the S&P 500 fell 0.45% and the equal-weight S&P proxy (RSP) fell almost exactly as much (-0.49%), unlike Monday's dispersion (see Movers) where the average stock was flat while a handful of AI-hardware names did all the damage. That broad-based softness is what a garden-variety pre-Fed, pre-decision de-risking day looks like, not a sector-specific rotation. And credit — the market this system leans on hardest to separate a real risk event from routine noise — stayed calm: high-yield spreads ticked up 6bp to 2.71% but remain comfortably unflagged (z -0.55), investment-grade spreads were flat (z +0.49). Coinbase's slide, in other words, reads exactly as the reporting frames it — a regulatory setback plus ordinary event-eve caution — not a sign of broader credit stress bleeding into risk assets (§4C: stated as the data-supported read, not asserted as the only possible cause).
dashboard_lag_note: Observation dates in parentheses where they trail Tuesday's 2026-09-15 close: TIPS real yield, breakeven, both credit-spread series, and SOFR publish a day behind (§5), dated Monday 09-14. Fed balance sheet and TGA are the weekly Thursday H.4.1 release, dated Wednesday 09-09 this week. Treasury tenors (3m/2y/10y/30y), DXY, and ON RRP are same-day fresh via Treasury.gov/NY Fed. Flagged rows (⚑): higher (or lower) than on all but a handful of days in the past six months — see the Reading key below.
dashboard_interp_html: Every Treasury tenor flagged for a fifth straight day — the front end eased off its record, the belly and long end ticked back up. The 3-month bill (the bill that matures inside the Fed's own decision horizon, so it tracks Fed policy most directly) held at 4.11% (unchanged on the day) with its flag easing slightly to z +3.19 from Monday's all-time record of +3.37 — still this system's second-highest reading ever for any series. The 2-year rose 2bp to 4.67% (z +2.90, essentially flat vs. Monday). Further out, the 10-year rose 3bp to 5.00% (z +2.87, a fresh cycle high in level terms even as its statistical flag stayed roughly level) and the 30-year rose 2bp to 5.36% (z +2.20). In real terms: anyone with an adjustable-rate loan, a money-market fund, or cash parked in a CD or bond fund is pricing off a curve where every maturity this system tracks is still running hotter than all but a handful of days in the past six months, hours before the Fed itself weighs in. The curve's shape: 2s10s (the 2-year-to-10-year gap, a read on what the market expects from the economy) widened 1bp to 33bp but stays flagged (z -1.50, a hair inside the threshold); the 3-month-to-10-year spread widened 3bp to 89bp and re-entered flagged territory (z +1.53) after dropping out Monday — the front end catching back up toward the 10-year's own fresh high. Credit ticked but didn't flag — still the calm outlier heading into the decision. High-yield spreads (OAS — the extra yield investors demand to lend to junk-rated companies over the "risk-free" Treasury rate) rose 6bp to 2.71% (z -0.55, dated Monday) — the first upward move in a while, but nowhere near a flag. Investment-grade spreads held flat at 0.80% (z +0.49). The real yield (2.60%, dated Monday) stayed flagged (z +2.08) while the breakeven (2.37%, same date) remains unremarkable (z +0.49) — the real-rate side of the curve, not inflation expectations, is still doing essentially all of the flagged work (Unit 2 of this curriculum). Equities fell broadly rather than in a concentrated pocket: the S&P 500 fell 0.45%, the Nasdaq-100 fell 0.78%, the Russell 2000 fell 0.76%, and the equal-weight S&P proxy (RSP) fell almost exactly as much as the cap-weighted index (-0.49%) — unlike Monday, today's softness wasn't concentrated in a handful of large names (see Movers, below, and Story). Oil (WTI) jumped 4.4% to $105.83 and is now flagged (z +1.59, the first oil flag since early September) on the Saudi-pipeline story described in Story, above. Gold eased 0.4% and copper was roughly flat. ON RRP (overnight reverse repo, a gauge of spare cash parked at the Fed) fell by roughly half to $0.70bn — a large move in percentage terms but still well within this near-zero facility's normal noisy range (z -0.40, unflagged).
movers_html:
How this section works: all 503 S&P constituents scanned mechanically; a stock qualifies only by moving >4% (>2.5% for the 50 biggest) — never by seeming interesting. 27 name candidates and 1 sector divergence qualified Tuesday; cap is 3 names + 1 sector note.

SWKS +13.55% (90.00, from 79.26) — what happened: Skyworks Solutions' largest single-day gain this system has recorded, following a prior 10% decline. Stated reason: Yahoo Finance, 24/7 Wall St., and StocksToTrade/Timothy Sykes report two catalysts landing together: the pending Skyworks-Qorvo merger is reported nearing completion, awaiting only Chinese regulatory approval, and Apple's unveiling of the "Duo" — its first foldable iPhone, at the highest price point in the product line's history — generated an immediate supplier read-across for Skyworks as a key radio-frequency chip provider to Apple's mobile lineup; 24/7 Wall St. reports the same read-through lifted Qorvo (+7%) and Qualcomm (+4%) the same session. Why it matters: a real, same-day market test of premium-smartphone-cycle demand flowing through to chip suppliers — a consumer-hardware read-through, not idiosyncratic (§8: no view offered on investment merit).

COIN −10.10% (172.11, from 191.45) — what happened: Coinbase's sharpest single-day decline in several weeks. Stated reason: Investing.com and 24/7 Wall St. report the trigger was a failed U.S. Senate procedural vote on the CLARITY Act (crypto market-structure legislation), which split 50-50 — short of the 60 votes needed to advance — compounded by Bitcoin (-2.9%) and Ether declines and general de-risking ahead of today's Fed decision; CoinCentral and Blockonomi both separately report ARK Invest sold its Coinbase stake Monday. Why it matters: a live test of whether crypto-adjacent weakness is a political/regulatory and event-eve story or something broader — credit spreads (dashboard, above) show no sign of the latter (§8: no view offered on investment merit).

AXON −9.81% (442.08, from 490.18) — what happened: Axon Enterprise's sharpest decline this system has recorded. Stated reason: Tradingpedia and GuruFocus report Axon priced a $1.0 billion offering of 0% convertible senior notes, with proceeds earmarked partly for capped-call transactions to offset share dilution and the remainder for general corporate purposes; the offering itself, not any operating news, drove the move. Why it matters: idiosyncratic — no macro read-through. This is a single company's financing decision (public-safety technology, not AI-capex-adjacent), included here because the section reports factual moves mechanically rather than only the ones with a story attached.

Beyond the three-name cap: Revvity (+9.1%, margin-target commentary at a healthcare conference per Simply Wall St./Investing.com), Jack Henry (-6.4%) and Chipotle (-5.9%, reported by Yahoo Finance/24/7 Wall St. as profit-taking with no fresh company news attached) were the next-largest movers, alongside Carvana, Casey's, and Dollar Tree all down 5–6% without a common thread across today's search.

Sector note: Energy (XLE) +2.17% vs. SPY −0.46% → +2.63pp — stated reason: Al Jazeera and OilPrice.com attribute the move to WTI/Brent's push to a four-month high (Story and dashboard, above) on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline remaining offline after last week's attacks, an alternative route around the Strait of Hormuz; APA (+5.3%), Chevron (+2.6%), and Exxon (+2.6%) led the sector. Read-through: a clean, single-cause macro read-through — the same oil-supply story tested by new claim CL-0017, above — not a stock-picking note.
chart_of_day_why: The 3-month bill still carries this system's largest active flag (z +3.19, second-highest ever recorded) hours before the Fed's own decision — the cleanest single chart of a hike priced as close to a foregone conclusion, and the series both rule (a) (largest |z|) and rule (d) (today's calendar event) point to together.
tier3_html:
Daily read: SMH (this system's chip-fund proxy for AI capex) rose a modest 0.11% Tuesday, a pause rather than a reversal after Monday's 4.75% drop, while the AI-hardware read-through in today's Movers section (Skyworks, Qualcomm) was driven by a consumer-smartphone cycle story (Apple's foldable iPhone), not a data-center capex signal — worth distinguishing from the AI-capex-cycle question CL-0015 is built to test, since the two chip-demand stories (premium handsets vs. hyperscaler buildout) are related but not identical.

Financing watch: No new hyperscaler/neocloud debt issuance or vendor-financing structures surfaced in today's web search. Axon's $1 billion zero-coupon convertible offering (Movers, above) is a real example of the financing-structure mechanics this system's Tier 3 watches for (issuers raising capital via low/no-coupon convertibles when volatility and rates are elevated, a Unit 7 topic ahead), but it sits outside the AI-capex complex this system's cycle-level monitoring is scoped to, so it is not logged as a capex-cycle data point.
calendar_note_html: Today is the week's central event day. Before the open: Retail Sales (consensus +0.8% m/m, a sharp rebound from -0.6%) and Core Retail Sales (consensus +0.5% vs. -0.3% prior) at 8:30am ET, plus low-impact Import Prices, Business Inventories, and the NAHB Housing Index. Then, at 2:00pm ET, the Fed's rate decision and updated economic projections (the "dot plot"), followed by Chair Warsh's press conference at 2:30pm — markets price roughly a 93% probability of a 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00% (see Story, above, and CL-0016, Claims). This brief frames rather than predicts (§4E): a hike delivered as priced, with hawkish guidance, would likely read as confirmation of a five-session run of front-end repricing already in this system's data (today's chart of the day, above); a hold against a near-certain hike — or a hike paired with dovish guidance — would be the bigger surprise, and the 2-year and 3-month bill are the series most likely to move hardest on it either way. Tomorrow's morning run reconciles CL-0016 against today's actual close.
concept_title: Why flat credit spreads heading into a known event are informative, not just quiet
concept_html: Every earlier segment in this unit used OAS (the extra yield lenders demand over Treasuries for default and liquidity risk) to tell a real risk event apart from a false positive — a rate spike, a violent single-stock swing. Today hands a different, related case: a known, scheduled event (a Fed decision, with a probability the market has been pricing for weeks) sits a few hours away, and credit spreads are essentially flat. It would be easy to read that as "nothing to see" — but flat spreads heading into a scheduled catalyst are themselves a data point, not an absence of one. Corporate bond investors, like equity investors, can price a known event in advance; if today's decision were likely to surprise the market in a way that raised real default or liquidity risk — an unexpectedly large hike, a shock to the dot plot — credit would typically start drifting wider in the days before it, the way it sometimes does ahead of a contested earnings report or a close election. It hasn't: HY OAS ticked up 6bp but stays two-thirds of a standard deviation below its own trailing average, and IG OAS is flat. That is consistent with a decision the market genuinely believes is close to fully priced, which is a different (and generally lower-risk) situation than a coin-flip event credit hasn't yet reacted to. The distinction matters for tomorrow morning specifically: if the Fed delivers something close to what's priced, credit staying calm today is exactly what you'd expect in hindsight; if the Fed surprises hard in either direction, watch whether credit reacts alongside rates — that reaction, not the rate move alone, is what would tell you whether markets are pricing new risk or just repricing the path.
client_translation: "Corporate bond markets aren't nervous heading into today's Fed decision — and that's useful information, because it means professional lenders think this is priced in and won't cause real financial stress, which is different from an unexpected shock."
client_lens_html:
• "Is the Fed raising rates today? What does that mean for my accounts?" — Markets are pricing roughly a 93% chance of a quarter-point hike at 2:00pm ET, which would be the first hike since 2023. Practically: a hike tends to lift yields on new CDs and money-market funds — good for savers reinvesting cash — while pressuring the price of existing bonds and bond funds already in client accounts, especially longer-duration ones (see today's concept, above, for why credit markets aren't signaling extra worry about it). This system frames what to watch rather than predicting the outcome; tomorrow's brief will report what actually happened.
  • "Did you see Coinbase drop 10%? Is crypto in trouble again?" — The stated reason, per reporting, is fairly specific: a Senate procedural vote on crypto market-structure legislation (the CLARITY Act) fell short Tuesday, plus ordinary caution ahead of today's Fed decision — not a sign of broader financial stress. Corporate credit spreads, the market this system watches to catch real stress early, didn't move. Worth being direct: this system verifies the move and reports the stated reason, but offers no view on Coinbase or crypto as an investment.
  • "Gas prices are creeping up again — is that the Middle East thing again?" — Yes, per reporting: a Saudi pipeline that serves as an alternate route around the Strait of Hormuz has been offline since an attack last week, and oil pushed to a four-month high on it Tuesday. This system opened a new dated test today (CL-0017) on whether that holds or fades, the same discipline applied to the original Iran-related oil claim that confirmed earlier this month.
